analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC and soft money from federal elections, funds challengers, curbs gerrymandering, and cuts candidates' TV ad costs.
analysis.headline: A campaign finance overhaul with 35 Senate sponsors that would have banned PAC and soft money died in the Senate Rules Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican Senate bill would have overhauled how federal campaigns are financed: banning political action committees and soft money, letting party committees give challengers up to $100,000 in seed money, forcing broadcasters to sell candidates ads at their lowest rate, and barring incumbents from taxpayer-funded mass mailings in election years. It also set anti-gerrymandering standards with citizen lawsuits, restricted lobbyist-run contribution conduits, and created new federal crimes for election fraud and public corruption. The Senate Rules Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would see special-interest PAC money and unregulated soft money barred from federal elections and get stronger disclosure and enforcement. Non-incumbent challengers would gain up to $100,000 in party seed money, cheaper broadcast ads, and an end to incumbents' election-year franked mail. Ordinary citizens could sue over gerrymandered districts, and whistleblowers who expose public corruption would get protection and back-pay remedies.

how_it_helps.text: Bans PACs from federal elections — only individuals and party or candidate committees could contribute or spend, ending the structured flow of corporate, trade-association, and union PAC money to candidates.
Bans soft money — money raised outside federal limits and disclosure rules — from being used to influence any federal election, with allocation rules for mixed federal/non-federal party activity.
Gives non-incumbent federal candidates up to $100,000 in 'seed money' from their party's congressional campaign committee to help them get competitive early.
Requires broadcasters to sell candidates pre-election airtime at their lowest rate and bars stations from bumping candidate ads for paying commercials, cutting campaign costs.
Prohibits franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings by members running for reelection, ending a form of free incumbent self-promotion, and requires registration and public inspection of mass mailings.
Sets redistricting standards — equal population, compactness, keeping counties and cities whole, no diluting voters by party — and lets ordinary voters sue in federal court to enforce them.

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 10 years, to deprive citizens of honest government services or a fair election through fraud, and protects employees who report such schemes with reinstatement and triple back pay.

Strengthens enforcement: mandatory FEC civil suits on tie votes, a private right of action for candidates when the FEC deadlocks, mandatory civil penalties, and removal of the fine ceiling for knowing violations involving $2,000 or more.
Bars registered lobbyists from serving as contribution conduits and limits conduits to bundled contributions from no more than two people of the same employer or organization.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate, trade-association, and labor PACs lose their federal channel; lobbyists lose the conduit role; broadcasters lose premium ad revenue during campaign season; incumbent members of Congress lose election-year franked mail, the ability to shift campaign funds to office accounts, and heavily gerrymandered districts; labor unions face new notice, audit, and escrow conditions to keep their political communications; and politically active tax-exempt groups would lose tax-exempt status for federal campaign activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, unions, lobbyists, broadcasters, and incumbents

drawbacks.text: The bill has no public financing and no spending limits; instead it routes more money through political parties — contributions to party committees are exempted from the $25,000 annual aggregate limit and national party research and materials costs are excluded from the contribution/expenditure definitions — potentially concentrating financial power in the national party committees.

Labor unions could keep political communications and segregated funds only if they meet annual written notices to every employee, independent CPA audits verifying representation costs, and escrow-and-appeal procedures for challenged fees; a union that fails must finance those activities solely from voluntarily contributed segregated-fund money — conditions unions have historically opposed as burdens on worker-backed political speech.

Banning PACs outright could push money toward less traceable channels; the bill's own fallback provision concedes this possibility by capping non-connected PACs at $1,000 for any period the ban is not in effect.
The new private right of action, mandatory penalties, and expedited review provisions would likely increase campaign-finance litigation and FEC adversarial proceedings.

The redistricting section bars districts drawn with the intent or effect of diluting the voting strength of any party, a standard that courts could interpret in ways that cut against majority-minority or other districts, though the bill expressly states it does not supersede the Voting Rights Act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance this was a serious anti-special-interest reform: it eliminated the two largest unregulated money channels of its era (PACs and soft money), empowered challengers, and added real enforcement teeth, all at a direct cost to concentrated interests rather than to ordinary people. Its honest weaknesses are that it substitutes party committees for PACs as the main organized-money pipeline without spending limits, and that its union-related conditions and litigation mechanisms would have drawn years of legal challenge. It did less for ordinary voters than reform bills with public financing would have, but it was far from a giveaway to any industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1990 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never held a hearing or a markup, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Mitch McConnell introduced the Comprehensive Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1990 on May 9, 1990, joined by 34 Republican Senate cosponsors including the Republican leader Robert Dole.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs funded by corporations, trade associations, and unions, along with the lobbyists and incumbents who benefit from the existing campaign money system, were the winners: the status quo was preserved and no one had to change how federal campaigns are financed.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it the backing of three-quarters of the Senate Republican conference.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 9, 1990 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 35 sponsors and cosponsors was a Senate Republican (34 of 45 Senate Republicans), no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-run Rules Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill's centerpiece bans PACs from making, soliciting, or spending money in federal elections, ending the structured corporate and trade-association money pipeline to candidates. Their loss of a privileged access channel is precisely the influence reduction ordinary voters would gain.

Union separate-segregated-fund PACs would be banned like all others, and unions would face annual member notices, independent CPA audits, and escrow procedures to keep their political communications and voter drives — forfeiting those activities if they fail to comply. Unions' interest in unrestricted member-funded political spending runs against the bill's disclosure and consent aims, though the PAC ban hits their corporate counterparts equally.

With PACs banned, party committees become the main organized-money channel: they gain new authority to give challengers up to $100,000 in seed money, exemption of party contributions from the $25,000 aggregate limit, and expanded exemptions for national party research and materials costs. The bill deliberately rebuilds campaign finance around parties as a counterweight to special-interest PACs.

Stations would have to sell candidates pre-election airtime at the lowest rate charged to any advertiser and could not preempt candidate ads for paying customers, directly costing broadcasters revenue. What broadcasters lose in premium rates, candidates and voters gain in cheaper campaign communication.

Incumbents would lose election-year franked mass mailings, the ability to shift campaign funds into official office-expense accounts, and the protection of gerrymandered districts, while facing mandatory penalties and candidate-triggered lawsuits from stronger FEC enforcement. Each restriction targets an incumbent advantage over challengers.

Organizations intervening in federal campaigns would lose 501 tax-exempt status, and politically active groups could lose it if candidates solicit contributions for them in coordination. This curbs a shadow channel for campaign money but also restricts nonprofit voter-registration and civic activity.
The bill bars registered lobbyists and their firms from acting as conduits for contributions to federal candidates, cutting off a common bundled-money practice that connects access to giving.
